text: Given two strings, word one and word two, return the minimum number of operations to convert word one into word two. You may insert a character, delete a character, or replace a character.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — all three operations cost the same, one unit each, and I can apply them anywhere in the string? And either word can be empty?
Correct — unit cost, any position, and yes, empty is allowed. Lengths go up to five hundred.

Let me run through the example. Horse to ros is three: replace h with r, delete r, delete e. Notice the optimal answer mixes operations — it's not all replacements — so a greedy character-by-character pass won't cut it.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would recurse on the three choices at every mismatch, which branches three ways and blows up exponentially. This problem reminds me of two-string prefix DP: a grid where cell i, j only cares about the first i characters of word one and the first j characters of word two, and each cell depends on its neighbours. Let dp of i, j be the minimum operations to turn the first i characters of word one into the first j characters of word two. The elegant part is that the three operations map to the three neighbours of a cell.

When the two last characters differ, I take one plus the min of three sources. Up is a delete of word one's character. Left is an insert of word two's character. Diagonal is a replace. The rule is: whichever string an operation consumes, that index steps back. Delete only touches word one, so i retreats — up. Insert only touches word two, so j retreats — left. Replace touches both — diagonal. And when the characters match, they align for free: the cell copies the diagonal with no plus one.

Base cases are the distance to the empty string. The first column is i: delete all i characters of word one. The first row is j: insert all j characters of word two. So, the plan. One: build an m plus one by n plus one table and fill both edges. Two: fill row by row — free diagonal on a match, otherwise one plus the min of up, left and diagonal. Three: return dp of m, n. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Two loops set the edges, then a double loop fills the table: on a match, copy the diagonal; otherwise, one plus the min of up, left and diagonal, written as a single min over a three-element list. One thing worth flagging — the plus one sits outside the min, and it only applies to the mismatch branch. It's order m n time and space, and it compresses to order n with a single rolling row plus a temp that saves the diagonal before it's overwritten.
Why no plus one when the characters match?

Because a matching pair already aligns — no operation is needed to reconcile them, so I just inherit the diagonal unchanged. It's the only zero-cost transition in the table, and it's what lets the distance drop below the longer length. If I forced a plus one there, I'd be charging for characters that were already correct.

Let's dry-run horse to ros; expected three. The cell that matters is the last one: e differs from s, and the neighbours are up two, left three, diagonal three. So it's one plus two, three — and the minimum came from up, meaning the last operation is a delete. That matches. Corner cases: intention to execution gives five. An empty input gives the other string's length. And swapping the two words gives the same distance.

Let me think about complexity here. Time and space are both order m n, and space is reducible to order of the shorter length — I'd pick the shorter string as the inner dimension, which is safe because the distance is symmetric. Oh, one more thing — the structure generalizes cleanly. Weighted edit distance just replaces each plus one with per-operation costs — that's the spell-check and DNA-alignment model. And if replacement were banned, this collapses to m plus n minus two times the LCS length, since the common subsequence is what you keep and everything else is one delete or one insert. Replace is exactly the shortcut that separates this from LCS.

Excellent. Three things stood out. You mapped the three operations to the three directions with a crisp rule — whichever string it consumes, that index steps back. You explained the free diagonal precisely. And you connected it to LCS and weighted variants, which shows you see the family, not just the one problem. Strong hire.
